# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# A Careful Reading of the Two-Year Follow-up

This is the most informative document in the series. It reports a registered, controlled follow-up at 24 months. It adds a second hours measure, tests the meetings hypothesis under a pre-filed plan, and responds directly to both the Varga–Holm re-analysis and the meta-analysis.

Most of its conclusions hold. But the headline decline is overstated in two ways, and an unplanned event in the control group affects the decline estimate. The mediation result is described as "confirming" more than mediation analysis can confirm. A simple time accounting also suggests the meetings explanation may be stronger than the registered estimate says.

## Arithmetic checks

- **Per hour, timesheets:** 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8%.
- **Per hour, system logs:** 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%.
- **"About a quarter" decline:** 9.8/12.5 is 0.78, a fall of about 22%.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9/40.3 gives −13.4%, and 96.8/86.6 gives +11.8%.

The figures are internally consistent. One coincidence is worth asking about. The 11 continuing Halden organisations have a baseline of 40.3 hours, exactly the average Varga and Holm reported for the 27 organisations with time tracking. That may be chance, but it could also mean the wrong group's baseline was used.

## What the report gets right

**1. It resolves the "entirely an artifact" claim.** The 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised controls and a two-year horizon, the standards Varga and Holm themselves recommended. It finds +8.5% (95% CI 3.4 to 13.8). That is about as clean an answer as one trial can give.

**2. It correctly undercuts the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim.** All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which is the weakness I raised in the previous review. Their pooled estimate cannot speak to decay.

**3. The counter arm now has a controlled comparison.** Waits were 7.3 minutes in treated offices against 4.0 in controls, alongside a costed estimate of what restoring service would require. That makes the earlier coverage-bound finding concrete.

**4. It answers my earlier questions about meeting data.** It provides a baseline for meeting time: 7.4 hours in treated offices and 7.2 in controls. This confirms my earlier assumption that the two groups started at similar levels.

**5. The unplanned observation is reported with honest caveats.** The report correctly identifies the open question: reorganisation alone versus the hours cut acting as a forcing device. The trial cannot settle it.

## Problems

### 1. The control-group meeting audit biases the decay estimate

Two of the seven control offices cut their meetings in month 15. Their output per hour then rose about 4.1%. That is exactly the change the trial is measuring. The control group was supposed to show what happens without the intervention, and part of it adopted the mechanism.

If those two offices gained around 4%, the control-arm average rises by roughly 1 point. The treatment–control gap narrows by the same amount over the final nine months. That could account for perhaps a third of the measured decline from 12.5% to 9.8%. Part of the "fading" may be the control group improving rather than the effect wearing off.

The report should present the 24-month estimate both with and without these two offices. It should also say whether the audit was prompted by contact with treated offices, which is the kind of contamination that office-level randomisation was meant to prevent.

The audit result also says something about mechanism. Cutting meetings by 2.1 hours frees about 5.5% of a 38-hour week for other work. A 4.1% gain is about what simply reallocating that time would produce.

### 2. The headline mixes two hours measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". The 12.5% uses timesheet hours and the 8.5% uses system-log hours. The like-for-like comparison, given later in the text, is 12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets.

Mixing the measures makes the decline look like about a third instead of about a fifth. The summary should state the timesheet comparison.

### 3. The decay is no better established than the meta-analysis's "no decay"

The confidence intervals overlap heavily: +6.9% to +18.4% at nine months and +4.6% to +15.2% at 24 months. The report does not test whether the change is statistically significant. With 14 clusters, it probably isn't.

"Consistent with some fading" is fair. "Declined by about a quarter", stated as fact in section 5, goes further than the data allow. It is the reverse of the error the report correctly identifies in the meta-analysis. Add the control contamination in point 1, and the honest summary is this: the gain did not go to zero, and it may have declined somewhat.

The point estimate for output per employee did move from −2.1% to −3.4%. The direction is worth watching, but it is also within the margin of error.

### 4. The mediation result is stronger in the summary than the analysis allows

**"Confirms" is too strong.** Mediation analysis estimates how much of an effect runs through a pathway. That estimate is causal only if nothing unmeasured drives both the mediator and the outcome. The Limitations section admits this. The summary still says the analysis "confirms" the meetings pathway. Causation could also run the other way: well-run offices may both cancel meetings and be more productive.

**The test may reuse the data that generated the hypothesis.** The plan was registered at month 11, after the month-six exploratory finding. If the "larger sample of office-months" includes months 1–9, the confirmatory test partly re-analyses the data that produced the hypothesis. A clean confirmation would use only months 12–24. The report should say which months were used.

**Few clusters still limit inference.** Office-months are not independent. The effective sample is still 14 offices. The intervals of 28–66% and 2–34% need the small-cluster methods I raised for the nine-month report, and the report doesn't say whether they were used.

**The comparison between mediators is tilted.** Meeting time comes from calendars, which are fairly precise. Fatigue comes from a survey scale, which is noisier. A noisier mediator always appears to explain less. So the finding that meetings explain "less than half as much" as fatigue is partly a measurement artifact. Fatigue's 18% is probably an underestimate.

### 5. Simple time accounting suggests meetings may explain nearly all of the gain

Start from the treated offices' baseline of about 37.9 timesheet hours and 7.4 meeting hours. That leaves about 30.5 hours for other work.

At 24 months, hours are down 12% relative to control, to about 33.4. Meetings are at 3.9 hours, leaving about 29.5 hours. Non-meeting time therefore fell only about 3%. In control offices it was roughly flat.

Relative to control, non-meeting hours fell about 4% and output fell 3.4%. Output per non-meeting hour is then essentially unchanged, at about +0.6%. On this crude accounting, nearly all of the per-hour gain comes from moving time out of meetings. Very little would come from staff working faster in the time they spent on cases.

This conflicts with the registered estimate of 47% for meetings, 18% for fatigue and 35% unexplained. The accounting has real limits:

- Calendar entries are not attendance.
- Some cancelled meetings may have had value that shows up elsewhere.
- Mediation models and accounting identities measure different things.

Still, the authors should reconcile the two. If the accounting is broadly right, it matters for any employer. It implies most of the gain comes from reorganising time and could be available without cutting hours, which fits the control-office audit. It would also leave little room for the fatigue pathway.

### 6. It's unclear what the log measure captures

Log hours are called the "stricter" measure, but what do they include?

- If they exclude meetings, they measure time on cases. In that case they should have fallen only about 3%, in line with non-meeting time, not 11%.
- Since they fell 11%, staff presumably stay logged in during meetings and other work.
- Logged-in time can also include idle time, and miss offline work such as phone calls or paper files.

The report also needs to confirm that log data exist for the pre-trial period. The log measure was "added" at follow-up, and a difference-in-differences estimate requires a baseline. If the logs go back to before the trial, the report should say so.

### 7. Outcomes still missing after two years

- **Backlog and time to decision.** This is the most important gap. With output per employee at −3.4% over 24 months, backlogs could have grown. The paper does not report backlog size or time from receiving a case to deciding it. Statutory-deadline breaches were flagged as a risk at nine months and still are not reported.
- **Overtime cost.** Timesheets record claimed overtime, but its cost is not reported. Without it there is no cost per case for the discretionary offices, even though the report gives one for the counter offices.
- **Sick days.** The figure is still a count of days per FTE, so the possibility that fewer working days mechanically means fewer sick days remains unaddressed.

### 8. The Halden subset

**There is selection at three stages.** These 14 are the organisations that responded, out of the 23 that submitted records, out of the 61 that completed the pilot, out of 70 that enrolled. The report candidly calls the 11 continuers "survivors twice over". In fact there are at least three stages of selection.

**The figure isn't strictly an upper bound.** Survivorship pushes it upward, but with no control group, general economic conditions over two years could push it in either direction. "Optimistic estimate" would be more accurate than "upper bound".

**A simple intention-to-treat figure is missing.** Including the three reverters at their output at the time of reversion (88–91) would be easy and more informative.

**The marketing agency complicates the sector story.** A marketing agency reverted, citing client deadlines. The pilot classed marketing as knowledge work, and the meta-analysis would code it as discretionary. The summary groups it under "client-facing or coverage obligations". That stretches the category to fit the agency in. It supports the meta-analysis's point that the right unit is the role, not the sector. It also suggests that client-driven deadlines can make discretionary work behave like coverage-bound work.

**The attrition question is left unanswered.** R. Okafor, an author of the original Halden paper, is a co-author here. The report does not respond to Varga and Holm's finding that seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons. This was the most serious charge against the original paper, and this was the natural place to address it.

## Overall assessment

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain persists at 24 months, about +8.5–10% | **Well supported**, the cleanest evidence in the series. |
| The gain declined by about a quarter | **Overstated.** The intervals overlap, the headline mixes measures, and part of the decline may come from control offices improving. "May have declined somewhat" fits the data. |
| Per-hour gains are not entirely an artifact | **Supported**, for discretionary public-sector case work. |
| The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim was unfounded | **Supported.** |
| Meetings mediate 47% of the gain, which the mediation analysis "confirms" | **Partly supported.** The direction is plausible. "Confirms" is too strong. Simple accounting suggests the share may be higher, and fatigue's share is probably understated by measurement noise. |
| Coverage-bound reduced hours are not viable without extra staff | **Well supported**, including the cost estimate. |
| Halden continuers gained 11.8% per hour | **Optimistic estimate.** Selected at several stages, with no controls. |

## Where the five documents leave things

- **Discretionary work:** a 20% cut in scheduled hours becomes roughly an 11–13% cut in actual hours. Output per employee is slightly below control, about −2% to −3%. Output per actual hour is about 8–10% higher, persisting to two years and perhaps fading somewhat. Backlogs and overtime costs are still unmeasured.
- **Coverage-bound work:** service worsens, and restoring it costs about 9% more per contact. The county abandoned that arm.
- **Mechanism:** much of the per-hour gain, possibly most of it, comes from clearing low-value time such as meetings. Rest plays a smaller, real role.

The open question has narrowed. It is no longer whether reduced hours raise productivity. It is whether the gain comes from the shorter week itself, or from the reorganisation that the shorter week forces, which an employer might achieve without cutting hours.

The control-office audit hints at the answer but cannot settle it. Settling it needs a third trial arm that reorganises work without reducing hours. Every study so far has lacked one, and it is the obvious next experiment.
